Star Explorers, developed and published by Schmidt Workshops, is a deeply systems-driven space exploration game that reflects both the ambition and the rough-edged charm of largely solo indie development. It places players in command of a spacecraft in a procedurally generated galaxy where humanity’s survival depends on discovering a new habitable world. Rather than presenting a scripted narrative or tightly guided campaign, the game embraces open-ended exploration, scientific simulation, and survival mechanics, inviting players to chart their own course through an indifferent and often hostile cosmos.

The central premise is simple but compelling: Earth is gone, and it is your responsibility to find a new home among the stars. From that starting point, Star Explorers unfolds into a sprawling procedural sandbox. Star systems are generated with underlying scientific logic, taking into account stellar types, orbital distances, atmospheric conditions, and planetary composition. This pseudo-scientific framework gives exploration a sense of authenticity. Players are not just hopping between randomly skinned planets; they are evaluating environmental factors, scanning systems, and making informed decisions about which celestial bodies might be survivable. The result is a galaxy that feels unpredictable yet grounded in a consistent internal logic.

Planetary exploration forms the core of the experience. After locating a promising world, players descend to its surface in first-person perspective, where survival becomes immediate and personal. Oxygen levels, environmental hazards, temperature extremes, and limited resources all shape how long you can remain on the surface. Many planets are lethally inhospitable at the outset, requiring suit upgrades or specialized equipment before they can be safely explored. This progression loop—scan, evaluate, prepare, land, survive, upgrade—creates a satisfying rhythm that rewards patience and careful planning.

Combat exists within the broader exploration framework but does not dominate the experience. Hostile creatures and environmental dangers present threats, particularly in underground caves or alien ruins scattered across planetary surfaces. These subterranean spaces often contain valuable materials, blueprints, or rare resources, encouraging deeper exploration despite the risks. Weapons and tools serve practical purposes beyond fighting, allowing players to mine materials, unlock new areas, and interact with alien environments. The sense of discovery is heightened by the fact that many planetary features are procedurally generated, ensuring that each landing carries genuine uncertainty.

Resource management plays a critical role in shaping the game’s tension. Fuel consumption dictates how far you can travel between star systems. Oxygen reserves limit planetary excursions. Ammunition and equipment durability affect survival odds during dangerous encounters. Poor planning can leave you stranded in deep space or trapped on a hostile world. The game does not shield players from these consequences, and part of its identity lies in its unforgiving nature. Success feels earned because failure is always possible.

Progression is tied to crafting and technological advancement. As players gather materials and uncover blueprints, they gain access to improved suits, stronger equipment, and enhanced ship capabilities. These upgrades expand the boundaries of exploration, enabling access to planets that were previously too cold, too hot, or too toxic to survive. This gradual widening of survivable environments mirrors the thematic journey of pushing humanity’s frontier ever further into the unknown.

Visually, Star Explorers adopts a minimalist and functional style. It does not attempt to rival high-budget space simulators in graphical fidelity. Instead, its presentation prioritizes clarity and procedural diversity. Planetary surfaces, star systems, and interiors may appear simplistic at times, but the constant variation ensures that no two discoveries feel identical. The interface and menus can occasionally feel clunky, reflecting the realities of indie development, yet they remain serviceable once players acclimate to the systems.

One of the more distinctive touches is the use of procedural music generation. Rather than relying solely on static tracks, the game creates ambient soundscapes that adapt to different environments, reinforcing the feeling that each planet has its own identity. This subtle audio design contributes to immersion and complements the isolation inherent in deep-space exploration.

The game’s pacing is deliberately open-ended. There are objectives, but no heavy-handed narrative guidance pushing players from one checkpoint to another. Instead, the motivation comes from curiosity and survival. The vastness of the galaxy, combined with the unpredictability of what lies in the next system, drives exploration forward. This design choice will resonate strongly with players who appreciate sandbox freedom and emergent storytelling. However, those seeking tightly structured missions or cinematic storytelling may find the lack of directed narrative less engaging.

Ultimately, Star Explorers is a passion project that prioritizes systemic depth and exploration freedom over polish and spectacle. It offers a procedurally generated universe governed by scientific logic, layered survival mechanics, and meaningful progression systems. Its technical roughness and steep learning curve may deter some players, but for those willing to invest time and patience, it delivers a rewarding experience rooted in curiosity, risk, and discovery. In a genre often dominated by high-production space epics, Star Explorers stands out as a focused, uncompromising indie exploration game that captures the loneliness and wonder of venturing into the unknown.

Essa é uma análise que dói no coração em ser negativa, mas não vejo forma mais honesta de avaliá-la. Sei o quão difícil é para desenvolvedores solo ou equipes pequenas criarem jogos indie, que, inclusive, considero os mais criativos da indústria. No entanto, Star Explorers, apesar do potencial colossal e do estilo gráfico encantador, peca demais na execução.

Como o nome sugere, o jogo propõe uma exploração galáctica em um universo aberto e, inicialmente, transmite uma sensação maravilhosa de que há algo oculto a ser descoberto, um grande mistério, algo precioso escondido, enquanto o jogador avança sob uma falsa sensação de solidão, tensão e até terror psicológico. Parece que a qualquer momento algo maior pode surgir para impedir sua jornada. Infelizmente, essa sensação não se concretiza.

A jornada, seja no início ou no fim, é exatamente a mesma: extremamente vazia.

Não há nada para se descobrir além de algumas ruínas alienígenas, elementos químicos da tabela periódica, desertos vazios e cavernas que rapidamente revelam os padrões da geração procedural, sempre repetindo os mesmos encaixes. Se o objetivo era criar um universo realista, com planetas vazios, eventos naturais coerentes (tornados, meteoritos, vulcões, lagos de mercúrio, ácido ou lava, temperaturas condizentes com a distância da estrela), então esse objetivo foi cumprido. Ainda assim, mesmo quando surge uma cidade rara ou um planeta com alguma forma de vida, a sensação de descoberta se esgota na primeira imagem ao pousar, não há profundidade além disso.

Mesmo reconhecendo que o jogo não prometeu explicitamente algo diferente, minha avaliação negativa não se baseia apenas em expectativa frustrada ou gosto pessoal. Star Explorers carece de polimento, cuidado e, principalmente, capricho. As IAs são extremamente básicas, as animações são robóticas e sem naturalidade, e a jogabilidade se torna rapidamente repetitiva e exaustiva. As missões são poucas, cansativas e mais frustrantes do que desafiadoras, a ponto de eu sentir alívio quando a campanha terminou.

O jogo possui avaliações “Muito Positivas”, algo que sinceramente não consigo compreender. Um indício disso é que apenas 24% dos jogadores concluíram a primeira missão e somente 8,9% chegaram à segunda, o que sugere que muitos abandonaram o jogo após poucas horas.

Star Explorers tem um potencial gigantesco. Meu desejo sincero seria vê-lo expandido e desenvolvido com o cuidado que sua proposta merece. Por enquanto, resta acompanhar as atualizações e torcer para que esse universo, tão rico em potencial, deixe de ser tão pobre em conteúdo real.

L'idée de base est vraiment très bonne. Un peu de captive et de star control  mais en vue 3D première personne, on va d'étoiles en étoiles et de planètes en planètes afin de trouver de précieuses sources de carburant pour notre vaisseau mère (contenant pas loin de 1 milliards d'habitants, tout de même).

Le problème, c'est la réalisation. On se fait chier. Y'a rien à faire. Il parait qu'il y a des aliens où des créatures agressives, j'ai fait plus de 20 planètes sans rien rencontrer. Le début bastonne un peu mais rapidement on met suffisamment de sous de coté pour pouvoir réparer notre combinaison autant que nécessaire.

Il y a deux GROS GROS GROS problèmes:
-Il n'y a aucun contenu, c'est tout juste un jeu. On a 4 5 décors de planètes, deux intempéries (météores et tornades), et un type de cave. Et c'est BASTA. Ou alors il faut peut être jouer 100 heures avant de voir un truc intéressant, je sais pas, j'ai pas eu le courage.
-On n'a aucun contrôle sur l'exploration. Sur une planète, on ne fait que déambuler en espérant voir un point rouge sur notre mini map ou (extrêmement rare) apercevoir un coffre au loin. Conclusion, je me suis amusé les 2 premières heures et ensuite, l'ennui total et j'ai abandonné après une 10aine d'heures. Il suffit de voir les % de validation des trophées. 78% pour le premier trophée, ce qui veut dire que le jeu suscite un véritable engouement mais plus que 8,8% finissent la première mission, faisable en 3 4 heures. Star Explorers. A wonderful little space game rooted in exploration and discovery. 
If youre a fan of games like; the original 1984 Elite, Star Control 2 or if youve ever wondered what No Mans Sky would have been if it were created back in 1998, this might just be the game for you. 
(Sidenote: This game gave me serious, Voyage of the BSM Pandora vibes! If you know you know 😊)

Although you probably wont be doing much space trading, mining or following a deep narritive driven story through a galaxy. You will be, hurling through sectors of space, scanning star systems, landing on unique procedurally generated planets, discovering different alien life forms, exploring cave systems and destroyed alien spacecraft. All in an effort to find a new home planet for human life. 

Its simple yet charming low res graphics give it a cozy, classic feel thats hard to find these days. Theres no deep, complex tutorial that holds your hand for the first two hours of gameplay. Instead youre presented with brief mission objectives from the captain of a mothership, in need of fuel and special quest items. There IS a fairly linear and short mission path that you can follow to 'beat' the game. But the beauty of Star Explorers is that there is no end. You can explore the galaxy as you see fit. 

The gameplay loop of Star Explorers is simple and you have to be okay with seeing the same things over and over, Just like the space games of old. 
Fly to a solar system, scan planets, land on planets with a suitable enviroment, explore the terrain, caves, alien ruins and so on, Collect resources and return to the mothership to cash in your findings or turn in mission related items. 
What makes all this so great though, is that everything youre seeing is different everytime. Planet eviroments will be different, alien life will have a variety of temperments, Items you find will be unique. Even the music you hear when you touch down is randomly generated, depending on the planets characteristics!
All of this makes you truly feel like youre venturing deeper and deeper into unknown space. 

I could obviously go on and on praising this game and it all sounds pretty great. But, you have to remember, this game is made by one guy! 
Ive seen many glitches in the 10 hours of play that Ive logged. It took me a solid hour to really understand what I was even doing or to figure out how to use the star chart efficiently. The NPCs in the mothership dont just feel like clones of each other...they effectively are. The controls can be a bit clunky and Ive even experienced a couple of game breaking glitches unfortunatley. Resulting in the need to fully restart with a new save...That being said, for a game that will only cost you a few dollars, this doesnt take away from the hours of fun that you can have in this massive galaxy! On top of all that. The dev still seems to be pushing out regular updates! 

If youre looking for a fun, abstract space exploration give Star Explorers a try!

A good bit of fun for a low-cost resource-management-heavy space exploration sim.

Gameplay loop is essentially: (1) be broke (2) land on planet, (3) find caves or wildlife, (4) space suit gets damaged from wildlife/mistakes/environment, (5) run out of repair kits, (6) take out anger on the local wildlife so you can sell their organs for enough repair kits to get you to about a 85% full repair and hopefully to be able to afford some form of upgrade, (7) run out of money, (8) grumble about being broke again.

The Star Chart is hair-pullingly confusing [i]until you realize[/i] that targeting the sector sets your target [i]to the mission location sector[/i], that the overlay button shows said sector's outline in a big green cube and shows planet orbits when in-system piloting your ship, and that you need to navigate through the sector-star-planets tabs in that order. After getting the hang of that it becomes fairly easy to navigate between sectors and stars, but I can see the risk of this as a potential quit moment for a lot of people.

[u]Some Criticisms[/u]:
--The mouse sensitivity in the inventory menu and when navigating planet surfaces are not the same leading to awkwardness when trying to loot corpses or chests. Maybe I am doing something wrong, but I played with the menu setting which didn't seem to help.
--The gunplay feels gross and janky, but at least pistol and rifle ammo is cheap and reasonably abundant from the mothership so missing shots regularly doesn't feel too upsetting.
--I understand that the jetpack is moreso there for preventing the player from getting stuck, but it feels strange that it doesn't really propel you any faster in your direction of travel.

This game is a hot and sweaty fever dream straight from an alternate reality 1999. Playing this game feels like a game you played as a kid but can’t quite fully remember, existing on the edge of consciousness. A distorted and twisted memory of a game pulled from a parallel past and made real.

It’s wild, it’s loose, and I love it.

In a landscape of hyper-slick and smoothed over AAA blockbusters and AA indie darlings Star Explorer pulls back the curtain into a dream-like mirror realm and invites you to explore its alien systems - from the actual planets you’ll explore to the strange and often archaic way the game is presented and played.

The presentation of the game and the subject matter pair wonderfully here, I feel. There’s a real sense of discovery in this game not just because of visiting surreal alien planets, but from soaking in the art style, and navigating its System Shock 2-like menus and controls. Those of us who love to explore in order to unravel complexities are well served here, as everything from the gameplay, the UI and the art subvert everything which is happening elsewhere in gaming right now. Depending on your preferences this could turn you off the game, or you could find it somewhat refreshing as I have. A great palette cleanser to dip into between the Starfields and Cyberpunks of the world.

The game has a small but sharp learning curve, mainly owed to a unique presentation and design philosophy. But once you get into the groove of seeking planets, landing and scavenging, it’s a weirdly relaxing experience and it sucked me in. 

It took me just 10 hours to “complete” the main quest, but I feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface of what can be found. The game is short but infinitely re-playable - after completing the main quest you can continue to complete procedurally generated fetch quests which encourage you to explore the remaining locations on your star chart. Then when you feel like you’ve ran out of places to go (the star map is not infinite), you can start a new game and do it all over again with re-rolled stars. 

So far what I’ve seen of the planets has been impressive considering the scope of the game. With variations in atmosphere density, liquid type, surface type, temperature etc, all having an impact on the visuals of the planet and the experience you have when you land. While in other space games these often just exist as a number on a planet stats page, Star Explorers does a reasonable attempt to actually put you there, with often surreal and truly alien results. Thick atmospheres which feel like moving through water, pools of silvery and reflective liquid mercury, and meteors that rain down on low-atmosphere planets to name but a few details. 

The terrain generation seems deep enough to provide some fun spots and breathtaking views, but often you will be exploring planets with similar profiles for quest reasons, and thus seeing similar rock-formations or other repeated familiar sights. You have to push out into dangerous or unusual territory to really see everything the proc-gen has to offer - for better or worse. It would be nice if the main quest gave you the tools and reasoning to push out into more exotic territory to show this off. Currently the only reason you would upgrade your suit enough to push out to some of the more dangerous planets is mainly out of curiosity or to satisfy a proc-gen fetch quest. This isn’t a bad thing really as the game is a sandbox by design, but there’s not much external motivation to visit the wildly hostile locations, and I find that a missed opportunity.

While I’m making a wish list.. Mountains, rivers, ringed planets, starports/space stations, and EVA (perhaps to scavenge for resources on the surface of asteroids) would all make for great additions, but as it stands the game feels like a complete experience anyway.

I was genuinely surprised by a few gameplay additions this game has - which I will avoid spoiling. The game has a decent amount of detail and will occasionally throw a curve-ball which expands your opinion of it just a little bit further. In all, the core gameplay loop of searching for (and landing on) planets remains largely in focus, but there’s a few neat distractions thrown in for good measure which are always worthwhile.

Coming away from the game and my biggest impression is that it is utterly surreal. Surreal enough (either intentionally or not) that when I woke up the next morning after my initial late night playing session, it took me a good 30 seconds to determine to myself whether or not the game I played was in fact real. Smiling to myself when I remembered that it was, and I could look forward to playing it again. 

For now I’m satisfied with the 10 hours I’ve put into the game, and will look to return back when the open-world slog of some AAA adventure has me in need of freshening up.

"An Interstellar Dungeon Crawler" is a fair description of the game. As you explore and find (and scan) new planets, you'll land on the ones in which your space suit will protect you. You may find things like alien ruins on the surface and also possibly chests which contain valuable loot. As you'd expect, loot means better suits and weapons and upgrades. 

You'll especially need to find caves to explore and there is where you'll find various resources to craft new items (if you have the blueprints for them). They are also where you'll find the all-important fuel crystals you'll need to keep exploring.

Your "base" is a large space station that can travel called the Mothership. You can buy items from the various shops there and even obtain missions. If you should happen to find fuel crystals on a planet you can drop a beacon there that the mothership will move to even if you've collected all of the available fuel.

You will also possibly meet alien entities both in space and on planets. Some are friendly, some not. Unfriendly aliens might shoot on sight or they may simply say that you are not worth their time and that humankind will eventually be destroyed by them. If they have the time. :) This means also that you might be attacked in space by alien ships. If you win, you can board the ship to potentially find loot. You can also board friendly ships that don't attack and speak to the aliens. However, as you might expect, should you take loot from their ship they will turn hostile.

You also have the ability to mine mineral resources by shooting asteriods. This can be a life-saver if you are having trouble finding fuel as you can take these resources and sell them on the mothership where you may also purchase fuel if you have the funds.

Each play through will be different as all star systems are randomly generated. So, nice re-play value.

That said, the game can be a bit quirky at times though nothing that's a showstopper. One thing that, to me, is especially immersion breaking are the sounds of creatures that wander about planets. They make sounds but there is no logic to how far away the sounds are. If they sound far away, creatures can actually be quite close. And if they sound like they are right on top of you there may not even be one in sight.

The other thing that I'd like to see addressed at some point is the anti-climatic nature of completing the main objective of finding a new "Earth". This is accomplished both too easily and too soon, and it would be nice if after you call the mothership to this planet that there is some indication of colonization after the fact. You can keep playing even after you find "New Earth" but it feels pointless. Some of the neat artifacts that you find and can build take longer than finding New Earth, so they can also feel pointless unfortunately.

Even so, this game is well worth the money even if the dev never does another thing to it. But that's another thing to like, at least for now; because he does still work on it even 5 years after release.
